q1.attribution: —Historian's account of the Song dynasty's commercial revolution, 960–1279
q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE way in which the Song economy changed between 960 and 1279.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the commercial growth described in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE continuity in Chinese governance that persisted despite the economic changes described in the passage.

sample_answers.a: One change was the deep monetization of the economy: the Song state issued paper money and minted copper coins on an enormous scale, so taxes, wages, and long-distance trade increasingly ran on money rather than on barter or payment in kind.
sample_answers.b: One cause was technological innovation in production, especially the use of coal in iron smelting, which lowered costs and expanded the output of tools, weapons, and coinage metal, feeding urban markets and interregional trade.
sample_answers.c: One continuity was rule by a Confucian scholar-bureaucracy selected through civil service examinations. The state kept its centralized administrative structure and its ideological commitment to Confucian order even as commerce transformed daily life.

q1.stimulus: During the Song dynasty (960–1279), China experienced what historians call a commercial revolution. Iron production soared with the use of coal, paper money circulated alongside copper coinage, and cities such as Hangzhou grew to more than a million residents supported by regional markets and interregional trade. Yet this economic dynamism unfolded inside a political system that never wavered in its Confucian bureaucratic character: scholar-officials selected by examination still governed, and the state still claimed ultimate authority over commerce.

q2.attribution: —Adapted from Marco Polo, Venetian merchant's account of his travels in China, c. 1300
q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE feature of Hangzhou that Marco Polo emphasizes in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the passage reflects China's participation in Afro-Eurasian exchange networks in the thirteenth century.
parts.c: Explain ONE limitation of using a foreign merchant's account as evidence about Song China.

sample_answers.a: Polo emphasizes the city's extraordinary size and wealth — its countless inhabitants, lofty houses, and people dressed in silk.
sample_answers.b: The passage reflects exchange networks because a Venetian merchant was present in China at all: the Silk Roads and maritime routes of the Mongol era carried travelers, goods, and information between Europe and East Asia.
sample_answers.c: One limitation is that Polo wrote to impress a European audience, so he may have exaggerated Hangzhou's splendor; he could not read Chinese and viewed the city through an admiring but incomplete foreigner's lens.

q2.stimulus: Hangzhou is without doubt the finest and most splendid city in the world. The houses are lofty and handsome, and the people dress in silk. So great is the multitude of its inhabitants that they cannot be counted, and the streets are kept clean and orderly.

q3.attribution: Map of Northern Song China, c. 1100
q3.directions: Use the map below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE geographic feature of the Song state shown on the map.
parts.b: Explain ONE way the Song dynasty's geographic position affected its economic development.
parts.c: Explain ONE continuity in the political organization of China visible on the map compared with earlier imperial dynasties.

sample_answers.a: The map shows the Song controlling only the eastern portion of historic China, with the Liao state occupying the north and Western Xia the northwest — China proper was divided among rival states.
sample_answers.b: Cut off from the Central Asian overland routes by the Liao and Xia, the Song turned to the sea, expanding maritime trade through ports such as Quanzhou and Guangzhou, which funded the state through customs revenue.
sample_answers.c: The map shows a single centralized imperial state with a capital administering a defined territory through provinces — the same centralized bureaucratic empire model used since the Qin and Han, even though its borders had shrunk.

q3.stimulus: Map of Northern Song China circa 1100, showing the imperial territory with its capital at Kaifeng, the neighboring Liao state to the north and Western Xia to the northwest, and major cities and rivers.
